extracted.intended_audience: psychologists, researchers, clinicians, and students studying humor, personality, and well-being
extracted.subtask_description: Classifying instances of humor by their social function using Martin et al.'s four-style framework (affiliative, self-enhancing, aggressive, self-defeating). Useful for research, assessment, or clinical interpretation of humor's relation to well-being and relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two orthogonal dimensions (Target and Valence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor styles vary along two orthogonal dimensions: Target — humor directed at self vs. humor directed at others/relationships; Valence — benign/adaptive uses vs. harmful/maladaptive uses. This produces four cells (self vs other crossed with adaptive vs maladaptive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two axes to place a humor instance into one of four style cells (self-enhancing, self-defeating, affiliative, aggressive). The framework is functional (about purpose/effect), not about content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliative humor (adaptive, other-directed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying funny things, telling jokes, witty banter. Goal: amuse others, ease tension, strengthen bonds. Does not denigrate self or others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: friendly teasing in a warm group, storytelling that amuses and connects. Correlates with extraversion, cheerfulness, and social support. Anti-patterns: denigrating jokes or sarcasm that harm relationships would not be affiliative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-enhancing humor (adaptive, self-directed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining a humorous perspective on adversity; amusing oneself even when alone. A coping use of humor (closely related to Freud's 'humor proper').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: supports coping and well-being. Correlates with self-esteem, optimism, and lower depression and anxiety. Example: reframing a stressful event with wry amusement to reduce its emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive humor (maladaptive, other-directed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sarcasm, ridicule, teasing, disparagement used to manipulate, criticize, or put others down; compulsive teller of offensive jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: damages relationships or asserts dominance. Correlates with hostility, neuroticism, and lower agreeableness. Anti-patterns: when similar content is used within mutual-love contexts it may be affiliative rather than aggressive (context matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-defeating humor (maladaptive, self-directed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive self-deprecation; allowing oneself to be the butt of jokes to gain acceptance; avoiding real issues through humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: may sacrifice one's dignity to connect or avoid intimacy; associated with depression, anxiety, low self-esteem, and neediness. Distinguish genuine light self-deprecation (may be affiliative) from self-defeating uses that compensate for deficits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional criteria for placing a humor instance
rubrics_metrics.description: To classify a particular humor act, ask: (1) Who is the target? Self, others, or no one in particular? (2) What is the social effect? Does it strengthen or damage relationships? (3) What is the psychological effect on the user? Does it support coping/well-being or compensate for deficit?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these functional questions rather than relying on text alone. The same joke text can serve different styles depending on speaker intent, target attachment, and audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-neutral classification (function over content)
rubrics_metrics.description: The classification is about function, not content: a dirty joke is not inherently aggressive; a self-deprecating remark is not inherently self-defeating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: self-deprecation that is genuinely good-natured = affiliative; self-deprecation as a defense against intimacy = self-defeating; roast humor in a context of mutual love = affiliative; same roast in a context of resentment = aggressive. Always consider intent, context, and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: What the HSQ framework excludes
rubrics_metrics.description: HSQ is not a pure structural theory: it tells you nothing about what makes a joke 'land' (i.e., what makes a joke be perceived as funny), only about what social purpose the joker is using humor to serve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use the HSQ to evaluate joke quality, comedic timing, or technical funniness; use it to infer social/psychological function and probable correlations with personality and well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic questions for any humor instance
rubrics_metrics.description: Toward whom is the humor directed? Does it maintain or damage the dignity of self/other? Does it serve coping or evasion? Does it serve connection or distance?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four concise diagnostic probes operationalize the functional criteria and help determine which of the four styles an instance most likely represents. Consider speaker intent, target attachment, and audience response when answering.
